title: Beige Book — October 14, 2026
html:
Official report: Summary · Full PDF Local PDF: 2026-10-14 Beige Book.pdf

Overall economic activity

Growth was uneven: two Districts reported moderate growth, three modest, four slight, and three little or no change. Manufacturing led in Dallas, and most other Districts saw modest to moderate manufacturing gains. Firms expect slight growth ahead, with persistent uncertainty. The report was prepared at the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia.

Consumer spending

Consumer spending was flat to slightly lower and was mostly driven by higher-income households. Auto sales were flat to lower. Tourism grew overall, though Boston, Minneapolis, and San Francisco reported weaker sales from Canadian visitors.

Labor markets

Employment was little changed. Shortages persisted for specialized, technical, and skilled trade workers. Five Districts reported that some firms cut staffing through attrition, delayed hiring, or expected less job creation after investing in AI. Wage growth ranged from slight to moderate, with cost-of-living demands and rising benefit costs adding pressure.

Prices

Price growth was robust in three Districts, moderate in eight, and modest in one, with four Districts reporting an acceleration. Higher oil prices affected every District, and diesel costs and fuel surcharges spread costs through supply chains. Tariffs, insurance, and other commodities also added pressure. Consumer-facing firms faced tighter margins as price-sensitive customers resisted increases. Firms expect further price increases as contracts and hedges are renegotiated.

Notable themes

  • Energy/oil: higher oil and diesel costs hit every District and are expected to keep feeding through.
  • AI: now cited in five Districts as a reason for lower staffing or slower hiring.
  • Tariffs and insurance: continuing cost pressures.
  • Uncertainty: persistent, including geopolitical and trade uncertainty (Dallas).
  • Tourism: up overall, but fewer Canadian visitors in some Districts.

District highlights

  • Boston: Slight expansion; flat consumer spending; weaker home sales; sharply higher home heating oil prices.
  • New York: Slight increase led by manufacturing; rising costs; selling prices at the high end of moderate.
  • Philadelphia: Slight growth; modest hiring; moderate wage and price increases.
  • Cleveland: Modest growth; moderate manufacturing demand; retailers hurt by fuel prices; robust selling price growth.
  • Richmond: Moderate growth; solid consumer spending; strong hotel occupancy; flat manufacturing.
  • Atlanta: Modest growth; flat employment; moderate prices; residential real estate up moderately.
  • Chicago: Flat activity; modest manufacturing gains; tighter financial conditions; lower farm income expectations.
  • St. Louis: Modest growth; unchanged employment; robust price increases; rising health care costs.
  • Minneapolis: Slight growth; higher employment; slightly lower consumer spending; moderate manufacturing gains.
  • Kansas City: Steady, subdued conditions with pockets of strong demand; diesel and shipping costs the main concern.
  • Dallas: Moderate expansion; strong manufacturing and prices; geopolitical and trade uncertainty.
  • San Francisco: Broadly steady; staffing held; moderate prices; softer retail; slight weakness in agriculture, residential real estate, and financial services.

Read-through for SPY

  • Flat-to-lower consumer spending with prices re-accelerating in four Districts is a stagflation-tinged mix that limits room for rate relief.
  • Oil and diesel costs expected to keep passing through contracts point to continued margin pressure, especially for consumer-facing firms.
  • AI-driven productivity is beginning to show up as slower hiring, a potential margin positive for large companies but a soft spot for jobs.
